name: process_vm_writev
synopsis: ssize_t process_vm_readv(pid_t pid, const struct iovec *local_iov, unsigned long liovcnt, const struct iovec *remote_iov, unsigned long riovcnt, unsigned long flags);
ssize_t process_vm_writev(pid_t pid, const struct iovec *local_iov, unsigned long liovcnt, const struct iovec *remote_iov, unsigned long riovcnt, unsigned long flags);
description: The process_vm_writev system call transfers data from the address space of the calling process to the address space of another process specified by PID. It uses iovec structures to define the memory regions for the transfer, and the data moves directly between the processes without passing through kernel space.

parameters.name: pid
parameters.description: The process ID of the remote process.

parameters.name: local_iov
parameters.description: Pointer to an array of iovec structures describing the local memory regions to read from.

parameters.name: liovcnt
parameters.description: The number of elements in the local_iov array.

parameters.name: remote_iov
parameters.description: Pointer to an array of iovec structures describing the remote memory regions to write to.

parameters.name: riovcnt
parameters.description: The number of elements in the remote_iov array.

parameters.name: flags
parameters.description: Currently unused and must be set to 0.

return_value.success: Returns the number of bytes written, which may be less than requested if a partial write occurred
return_value.failure: Returns -1 on error, and errno is set

errors.description: The memory described by local_iov is outside the caller’s accessible address space.
The memory described by remote_iov is outside the accessible address space of the process pid.
The sum of the iov_len values of either local_iov or remote_iov overflows a ssize_t value.
liovcnt or riovcnt is too large.
Could not allocate memory for internal copies of the iovec structures.
The caller does not have permission to access the address space of the process pid.
No process with ID pid exists.

bugs: The data transfers are not guaranteed to be atomic in any way.
